# Let's find a hurricane you're interested in.

LIVE For live storm tracks, please visit the [National Hurricane Center](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/).

## Powerful Search

With over 13,000 storm tracks on record, it could be easy to get lost. Fortunately the tool’s search box lets you quickly search a specific location, storm, year, or ocean basin. It’s equally easy to save this information for future use and to share with others.

[Video 1](https://coast.noaa.gov/hurricanes/buffer-BiI1oa0E.mp4)

## Increasing the Search Distance

Having trouble finding a storm that you know should be there? Increasing the search distance can help.

For example, Hurricane Harvey (2017) caused catastrophic flooding and over 60 deaths in the Houston area, but this storm track didn’t come within 90 miles of the city. Since the default search range is 60 miles, search results for “Houston” won’t include Hurricane Harvey. Increasing the search distance to 115 miles will rectify this.

[Video 2](https://coast.noaa.gov/hurricanes/storm-details-rZipUH6m.mp4)

## Get the Details

Clicking on a storm in the list or from the map will connect you to the details section. Here you will see the entire storm track and obtain data about the storm’s maximum wind speed and minimum pressure. You can also find links to a technical report and additional storm details when they are available.

For example, Hurricane Harvey (2017) caused catastrophic flooding and over 60 deaths in the Houston area, but this storm track didn’t come within 90 miles of the city. Since the default search range is 60 miles, search results for “Houston” won’t include Hurricane Harvey. Increasing the search distance to 115 miles will rectify this.

## Get the Details

Clicking on a storm in the list or from the map will connect you to the details section. Here you will see the entire storm track and obtain data about the storm’s maximum wind speed and minimum pressure. You can also find links to a technical report and additional storm details when they are available.

[Hurricane Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hugo "Hurricane Hugo") approaching South Carolina as a Category 4 hurricane on September 21, 1989

Since 1851, 132 [tropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone") or [subtropical cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone") have either directly or indirectly affected the state of [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), with the most recent being [Chantal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Chantal_(2025) "Tropical Storm Chantal (2025)") in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2025 Atlantic hurricane season").

*   July 1–2, 2022 – [Tropical Storm Colin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Tropical_Storm_Colin "2022 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall near [Hunting Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunting_Island_State_Park "Hunting Island State Park") as a minimal tropical storm on July 1. Up to 7.59 in (193 mm) of rain fell near [Wadmalaw Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadmalaw_Island "Wadmalaw Island").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Presbyterian_College_after_Hurricane_Helene%2C_September_2024.jpg/250px-Presbyterian_College_after_Hurricane_Helene%2C_September_2024.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Presbyterian_College_after_Hurricane_Helene,_September_2024.jpg)

Uprooted and damaged trees in [Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton,_South_Carolina "Clinton, South Carolina") following the passage of [Helene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Helene "Hurricane Helene")

Up to 8.14 in (207 mm) of rain fell in [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina"), and over 210,000 people lost power in the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-68)

*   September 27, 2024 – [Hurricane Helene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Helene "Hurricane Helene") passed near western South Carolina as a tropical storm, bringing flooding, high winds, and several tornadoes. Wind gusts reached 75 mph (121 km/h) in [Beaufort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaufort,_South_Carolina "Beaufort, South Carolina"), and up to 21.66 in (550 mm) of rain fell in [Rocky Bottom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Bottom,_South_Carolina "Rocky Bottom, South Carolina"). **Hurricane Floyd** was a powerful and destructive [tropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone") which struck the [Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas") and the East Coast of the United States. It was the sixth [named storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_named_tropical_cyclones "List of named tropical cyclones"), fourth [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane "Hurricane"), and third major hurricane in the [1999 Atlantic hurricane season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1999 Atlantic hurricane season"). Floyd triggered the fourth largest evacuation in [US history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_history "US history") (behind [Hurricane Irma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Irma "Hurricane Irma"), [Hurricane Gustav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Gustav "Hurricane Gustav"), and [Hurricane Rita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Rita "Hurricane Rita")) when 2.6 million coastal residents of five states were ordered from their homes as it approached. The hurricane formed off the coast of Africa and lasted from September 7 to 19, becoming [extratropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical "Extratropical") after September 17, and peaked in strength as a very strong Category 4 hurricane. It was among the largest [Atlantic hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_hurricane "Atlantic hurricane") of its strength ever recorded, in terms of gale-force diameter.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Legacy-1)

Floyd was once forecast to strike Florida, but turned away. Instead, Floyd struck the Bahamas at peak strength, causing heavy damage. It then moved parallel to the [East Coast of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States"), causing massive evacuations and costly preparations from Florida through the Mid-Atlantic states. The storm weakened significantly, however, before striking the [Cape Fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Fear_(region) "Cape Fear (region)") region, [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina") as a very strong Category 2 hurricane, and caused further damage as it traveled up the [Mid-Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_States "Mid-Atlantic States") region and into [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England").

The hurricane produced torrential rainfall in [Eastern North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_North_Carolina "Eastern North Carolina"), adding more rain to an area already hit by [Hurricane Dennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dennis_(1999) "Hurricane Dennis (1999)") just weeks earlier. The rains caused widespread flooding over a period of several weeks; nearly every river basin in the eastern part of the state exceeded 500-year flood levels. In total, Floyd was responsible for 85 fatalities and $6.5 billion (1999[USD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")) in damage. Due to the destruction, the [World Meteorological Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Meteorological_Organization "World Meteorological Organization")[retired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_retired_Atlantic_hurricane_names "List of retired Atlantic hurricane names") the name _Floyd_ and replaced it with _Franklin_.

Floyd originated from a [tropical wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_wave "Tropical wave") that exited the west coast of [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") on September 2. The wave moved generally westward, presenting a general curvature in its [convection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection_(meteorology) "Convection (meteorology)"), or thunderstorms, but little organization at first. By September 5, a center of circulation was evident within the convective system. Over the next day, the thunderstorms increased in intensity as they organized into a curved band. Aided by favorable [outflow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outflow_(meteorology) "Outflow (meteorology)"), the system organized further into Tropical Depression Eight late on September 7, located about 1,000 mi (1,600 km) east of the [Lesser Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Antilles "Lesser Antilles"). With a strong [ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_(meteorology) "Ridge (meteorology)") of high pressure to its north, the nascent tropical depression moved to the west-northwest, where environmental conditions favored continued strengthening,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) including progressively warmer [water temperatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_surface_temperature "Sea surface temperature").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-d2-3) On issuing its first advisory, the [National Hurricane Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hurricane_Center "National Hurricane Center") (NHC) anticipated that the depression would intensify into a hurricane within three days,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-4) a forecast that proved accurate.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) On its second advisory, NHC forecaster Lixion Avila stated that the depression had "all the ingredients...that we know of...to become a major hurricane eventually."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-d2-3)

Early on September 8, the depression became sufficiently well-organized for the NHC to upgrade it to Tropical Storm Floyd.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) The storm had a large circulation,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-5) but Floyd initially lacked a well-defined inner core, which resulted in only slow strengthening.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) The first [Hurricane Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hunters "Hurricane Hunters") mission occurred on September 9, which observed the developing storm.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-6) On September 10, Floyd intensified into a hurricane about 230 mi (370 km) east-northeast of the [Lesser Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Antilles "Lesser Antilles"). Around that time, the track shifted more to the northwest, steered by a [tropical upper tropospheric trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_upper_tropospheric_trough "Tropical upper tropospheric trough") north of Puerto Rico.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) An [eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_(cyclone) "Eye (cyclone)") developed in the center of the hurricane, signaling strengthening.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-7) On September 11, Hurricane Floyd moved through the upper-level trough, which, in conjunction with an [anticyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticyclone "Anticyclone") over the eastern Caribbean, disrupted the outflow and caused the winds to weaken briefly. The hurricane re-intensified on September 12 as its track shifted more to the west, steered by a ridge to the north. That day, the NHC upgraded Floyd to a major hurricane, or a Category 3 on the [Saffir-Simpson scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saffir-Simpson_scale "Saffir-Simpson scale").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)

[![Image 10: An animated map showing rain moving over North Carolina](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Floyd1999NCLandfall.gif/250px-Floyd1999NCLandfall.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Floyd1999NCLandfall.gif)

Radar imagery of Hurricane Floyd making landfall in North Carolina.

Over a 24-hour period from September 12–13, Hurricane Floyd [rapidly intensified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapidly_intensified "Rapidly intensified"), aided by warm waters east of [The Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bahamas "The Bahamas"). During that time, the [maximum sustained winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_sustained_wind "Maximum sustained wind") increased from 110 to 155 mph (177 to 249 km/h),[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-8) making Floyd a strong [Category 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Category_4_Atlantic_hurricanes "List of Category 4 Atlantic hurricanes") hurricane. This was based a 90% reduction of an observation by the Hurricane Hunters, which recorded flight-level winds of 171 mph (276 km/h). Around the same time, the [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure") dropped to 921[mb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(unit) "Bar (unit)") (921[hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)"); 27.2[inHg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inch_of_mercury "Inch of mercury")).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) Around this time, [tropical cyclone forecast models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_forecast_model "Tropical cyclone forecast model") suggested an eventual landfall in the Southeastern United States from [Palm Beach, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palm_Beach,_Florida "Palm Beach, Florida") to South Carolina.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-9)

At its peak, tropical storm-force winds spanned a diameter of 580 mi (930 km), making Floyd one of the largest Atlantic hurricanes of its intensity ever recorded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Legacy-1) For about 12 hours, Hurricane Floyd remained just below Category 5 status while crossing The Bahamas. Late on September 13, the eye of the hurricane passed just north of [San Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador_Island "San Salvador Island") and [Cat Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_Island,_Bahamas "Cat Island, Bahamas"). On the next day, the hurricane made [landfalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landfall "Landfall") on [Eleuthera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleuthera "Eleuthera") and [Abaco islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abaco_Islands "Abaco Islands").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) During this time, Floyd underwent an [eyewall replacement cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyewall_replacement_cycle "Eyewall replacement cycle"), in which an outer eyewall developed, causing the original eye to dissipate near Eleuthera. This caused a temporary drop in sustained winds to Category 3 status, only for Floyd to restrengthen briefly to a Category 4 on September 15.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)

While approaching the southeastern United States, a strong mid- to upper-level trough eroded the western portion of the high-pressure ridge, which had been steering Floyd for several days. The break in the ridge caused Floyd to turn to the northwest. After the hurricane completed its eyewall replacement cycle, Floyd had a large 57 mi (93 km) eye. The large storm gradually weakened after exiting The Bahamas, due to drier air and increasing wind shear. On September 15, Floyd paralleled the east coast of Florida about 110 mi (170 km) offshore, as it accelerated to the north and north-northeast. At around 06:30 UTC on September 16, Hurricane Floyd made [landfall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landfall "Landfall") in [Cape Fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Fear_(region) "Cape Fear (region)"), [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina") with winds of 105 mph (169 km/h), a Category 2. The eyewall had largely dissipated by that time. Continuing northeastward along a cold front, Floyd moved through eastern North Carolina and southeastern Virginia, weakening to tropical storm status by late on September 16. The storm gradually lost its tropical characteristics as it quickly moved through the [Delmarva Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmarva_Peninsula "Delmarva Peninsula"), eastern New Jersey, [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island"), and New England. Late on September 17, Floyd transitioned into an [extratropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone "Extratropical cyclone") near the coast of southern [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine"). The storm continued to the northeast, passing through New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland on September 18. On the following day, a larger extratropical storm over the North Atlantic Ocean absorbed what was once Hurricane Floyd.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)

## Preparations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Preparations")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Andrew-Floyd.jpg/250px-Andrew-Floyd.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andrew-Floyd.jpg)

Visual comparison of Hurricane Floyd with [Hurricane Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Andrew "Hurricane Andrew") while at similar positions and nearly identical intensities

When Floyd posed a threat to the Lesser Antilles, a [tropical storm watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_warnings_and_watches "Tropical cyclone warnings and watches") was issued for [Antigua and Barbuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_and_Barbuda "Antigua and Barbuda"), [Anguilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anguilla "Anguilla"), [Saint Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Martin_(island) "Saint Martin (island)"), and [Saint Barthelemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Barthelemy "Saint Barthelemy").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)

On September 12, a tropical storm warning and a hurricane watch was issued for the [Turks and Caicos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turks_and_Caicos_Islands "Turks and Caicos Islands") and the southeast Bahamas. A day later, the Bahamas issued a hurricane warning for the central and northwestern parts of the archipelago.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)[Nassau International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nassau_International_Airport "Nassau International Airport") shut down during the hurricane. Hotels provided tourists riding out the storm with candles.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-reut914-10)

While Floyd was near peak intensity on September 13, the NHC noted the differing forecasts by [computer models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_prediction_models "Tropical cyclone prediction models"), which anticipated the hurricane could hit anywhere from [Palm Beach, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palm_Beach,_Florida "Palm Beach, Florida") to South Carolina.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-11) That day, the agency issued a hurricane warning from [Florida City, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_City,_Florida "Florida City, Florida") to [Brunswick, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick,_Georgia "Brunswick, Georgia"). Ultimately, nearly all of the [East Coast of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") from [Florida City, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_City,_Florida "Florida City, Florida"), to [Plymouth, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Massachusetts "Plymouth, Massachusetts"), was under a hurricane warning. The last time such widespread hurricane warnings occurred was during [Hurricane Donna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Donna "Hurricane Donna") in 1960.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) Due to the hurricane's threat, around 2.6 million people evacuated from Florida to the Carolinas, which was the largest peacetime [evacuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_evacuation "Emergency evacuation") in U.S. history at the time.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-extremes0999-12)

Florida governor [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush "Jeb Bush") declared a state of emergency in anticipation of Floyd's approach.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-reut914-10) More than 1 million people in the state were ordered to evacuate, including 272,000 in [Miami-Dade County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami-Dade_County "Miami-Dade County"). Navy ships and military aircraft flew away from the state, and [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") reduced its crew.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-13)[Walt Disney World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_World "Walt Disney World") closed for the first time in its history due to the storm.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-15)[SeaWorld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaWorld "SeaWorld") was also closed. Flights were canceled across southern Florida. A state of emergency was also declared in Georgia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-16) A [hurricane warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_force_wind_warning "Hurricane force wind warning") was issued for the North Carolina coastline 27 hours prior to landfall.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) Officials opened at least 40 emergency shelters in North Carolina.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-NCNCDC-17)

[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/87/Floyd-_Traffic.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Floyd-_Traffic.jpg)

Evacuation on [Interstate 26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_26 "Interstate 26")

In [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), the [Baltimore Orioles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_Orioles "Baltimore Orioles") postponed a baseball game.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-18) Pennsylvania governor [Tom Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Ridge "Tom Ridge") declared a state of emergency for eastern Pennsylvania.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Mt_Holly-19) A state of emergency was declared in Delaware, Maryland, and New Jersey, prompting schools statewide to be shut down on September 16. In Delaware, about 300 people evacuated.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ncdcmd2-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-dencdc-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-njncdc-22) Across New York, schools were closed and flights were cancelled.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nyncdc-23) This included the first school closures for New York City since the [Blizzard of 1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_1996_United_States_blizzard "January 1996 United States blizzard").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-24) The [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") issued flood watches as far north as Maine.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-25)

In Atlantic Canada, the [Canadian Hurricane Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Hurricane_Centre "Canadian Hurricane Centre") issued 14 warnings related to Floyd, generating significant media interest. About 100 [Sable Offshore Energy Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sable_Offshore_Energy_Project "Sable Offshore Energy Project") employees were evacuated to the mainland. In southwestern Nova Scotia, 66 schools were closed, and provincial ferry service with [Bar Harbor, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_Harbor,_Maine "Bar Harbor, Maine") was canceled.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ec-26)

With a death toll of 85, Hurricane Floyd was the deadliest United States hurricane since [Hurricane Agnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Agnes "Hurricane Agnes") in 1972. The storm was the third-costliest hurricane in the nation's history at the time, with monetary damage estimated at $6.5 billion (1999 USD); it ranked the 19th costliest as of 2017.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-27) Most of the deaths and damage were from inland, freshwater flooding in eastern North Carolina.

### Caribbean

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Caribbean")]

Around when Floyd first became a hurricane, its outer bands moved over the Lesser Antilles.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-28)

While Floyd moved through the Bahamas, a station in [Nassau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nassau,_Bahamas "Nassau, Bahamas") recorded wind gusts of 78 mph (126 km/h), along with sustained winds of 64 mph (102 km/h). [Grand Bahama Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Bahama_Island "Grand Bahama Island") recorded a [tide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_surge "Storm surge") of 5.27 ft (1.61 m) above [mean sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geodetic_Vertical_Datum_of_1929 "National Geodetic Vertical Datum of 1929"). Floyd also dropped heavy rainfall across the Bahamas, peaking at 9.32 in (237 mm) in Little Harbour in the Abacos.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) The hurricane also produced waves estimated up to 50 ft (15 m) in height.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-extremes0999-12) A 20 ft (6.10 m) storm surge inundated many islands with over five ft (1.5 m) of water throughout.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-baha-29) The wind and waves toppled power and communication lines, severely disrupting electricity and telephone services for days. Damage was greatest at [Abaco Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abaco_Island "Abaco Island"), [Cat Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_Island_(Bahamas) "Cat Island (Bahamas)"), [San Salvador Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Salvador_Island "San Salvador Island"), and [Eleuthera Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleuthera_Island "Eleuthera Island"), where Floyd uprooted trees and destroyed a significant number of houses.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-30) Numerous restaurants, hotels, shops, and homes were devastated, severely limiting in the recovery period tourism on which many rely for economic well-being.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-31) Damaged water systems left tens of thousands across the archipelago without water, electricity, or food. One person drowned in [Freeport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeport,_Bahamas "Freeport, Bahamas"). A few injuries were reported.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-baha-29)

### Southeastern United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Southeastern United States")]

Main article: [Effects of Hurricane Floyd in Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_Hurricane_Floyd_in_Florida "Effects of Hurricane Floyd in Florida")

For several days, Floyd paralleled the east coast of Florida, producing about $50 million in damage, mostly in [Volusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volusia "Volusia") county. There, high winds and falling trees damaged 337 homes. The highest recorded wind gust in the state was 69 mph (111 km/h) in [Daytona Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytona_Beach "Daytona Beach"). [Beach erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach_erosion "Beach erosion") affected much of the state's Atlantic coast. The most significant effects were in [Brevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brevard_County,_Florida "Brevard County, Florida") and [Volusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volusia "Volusia") counties, where waves damaged houses and piers. Rainfall in the state reached 3.2 in (81 mm) in [Sanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanford,_Florida "Sanford, Florida").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-sd-33) When Floyd passed by the area, [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") only reported light winds with minor water intrusion. Overall damage was minor and was repaired easily.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-34)

Farther north in [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), Floyd produced wind gusts of 53 mph (85 km/h) at [Savannah International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah_International_Airport "Savannah International Airport"). The winds knocked down a few trees and power lines near the coast, but statewide damage was minimal. In [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah,_Georgia "Savannah, Georgia"), the hurricane produced tides 3.3 ft (1.0 m) above normal. Rainfall was light in the state, reaching 0.85 in (22 mm) in [Newington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newington,_Georgia "Newington, Georgia").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-35)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)

Tropical storm force winds affected the entirety of the South Carolina coastline, with statewide damage estimated at $17 million. Sustained winds reached 54 mph (87 km/h) at the [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina") National Weather Service Office, which also recorded wind gusts of 85 mph (137 km/h). The winds destroyed a few roofs and knocked down thousands of trees, leaving more than 200,000 people without electricity. The hurricane produced above normal tides along the coast, reaching 10.1 ft (3.1 m) above normal in [Charleston Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston_Harbor "Charleston Harbor"). The waves caused minor to moderate beach erosion. At [Myrtle Beach International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtle_Beach_International_Airport "Myrtle Beach International Airport"), Hurricane Floyd dropped 16.06 in (408 mm) of rainfall, the highest recorded in the state.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-36)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)

### North Carolina

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: North Carolina")]

[![Image 13: A picture of a damaged beach house](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Floyd-_Property_Damage.gif/250px-Floyd-_Property_Damage.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Floyd-_Property_Damage.gif)

Coastal property damage at [Pine Knoll Shores, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pine_Knoll_Shores,_North_Carolina "Pine Knoll Shores, North Carolina")

In North Carolina, Floyd killed 52 people and left more than $3 billion in damage, becoming the costliest hurricane in the state's history. It retained this status until 2018, when [Hurricane Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Florence "Hurricane Florence") left $22 billion in damage in the state.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nws-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-38) Of the 52 statewide deaths, at least 23 were near or in flooded vehicles, 6 drowned in a capsized boat, and 1 was a fatal car accident.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-assess-39) Throughout the state, the hurricane left 500,000 people without electricity. Floyd damaged 56,000 homes statewide, with 17,000 homes left uninhabitable, and another 7,000 homes destroyed.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nws-37) About 10,000 people stayed in temporary shelters after the storm.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-extremes0999-12) There was also extensive agriculture damage in the state, estimated at $812.6 million. The floods killed more than 2.9 million poultry, 30,500 hogs, and 880 cattle.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-sog-40)

Less than two weeks after [Tropical Storm Dennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dennis_(1999) "Hurricane Dennis (1999)") affected the state, Floyd brought additional rainfall and saturated grounds.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-usgs-41) A [pluviometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluviometer "Pluviometer") north of [Southport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southport,_North_Carolina "Southport, North Carolina") recorded 24.06 in (611 mm) of rainfall during the storm, the highest rainfall total in the country associated with Floyd.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-WPCMAX-42) Much of east-central North Carolina received more than 12 in (300 mm) of precipitation, with a 24-hour total of 15.06 in (383 mm) recorded in Wilmington, breaking the 128 year record.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) Nearly [every river basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rivers_of_North_Carolina "List of rivers of North Carolina") east of [Raleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh,_North_Carolina "Raleigh, North Carolina") recorded [500 year floods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_period "Return period"). Water gauges at 39 locations reached record levels in the state, with record floods along the [Cape Fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Fear_River "Cape Fear River"), [Chowan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chowan_River "Chowan River"), Neuse, [Pee Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pee_Dee_River "Pee Dee River"), [Tar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tar_River "Tar River"), and [Waccaaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waccamaw_River "Waccamaw River") rivers.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ilm-43) The most significant flooding occurred along the Tar River at [Tarboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarboro,_North_Carolina "Tarboro, North Carolina"), which crested 29.74 ft (9.06 m) above flood stage in [Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenville,_North_Carolina "Greenville, North Carolina"). The floods severely damaged the communities of Tarboro and [Princeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeville,_North_Carolina "Princeville, North Carolina").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ilm-43) Floods submerged Princeville for 12 days.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-44) Damages in [Pitt County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitt_County "Pitt County") alone were estimated at $1.6 billion.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-extremes0999-12) When a river gauge on the Tar near Greenville malfunctioned, a National Weather Service employee took manual observations every hour to document the record flood. The Neuse River at [Goldsboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldsboro,_North_Carolina "Goldsboro, North Carolina") crested at 28.85 ft (8.79 m), breaking the record set after [Hurricane Fran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fran "Hurricane Fran") in 1996.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-assess-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-usgs-41) Much of [Duplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duplin_County,_North_Carolina "Duplin County, North Carolina") and [Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greene_County,_North_Carolina "Greene County, North Carolina") counties were under water.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-NCNCDC-17) Of the state's eastern rivers, only the [Lumber River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumber_River "Lumber River") escaped catastrophic flooding.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-usgs-flooding-45)

The floods' coverage reached around 6,600 sq mi (17,000 km 2). Floodwaters closed nearly 1,000 roads in the state, including [I-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_95_in_North_Carolina "Interstate 95 in North Carolina") from [Johnston County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnston_County,_North_Carolina "Johnston County, North Carolina") to Virginia, [I-40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_40_in_North_Carolina "Interstate 40 in North Carolina") from [Sampson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampson_County,_North_Carolina "Sampson County, North Carolina") to [New Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hanover_County,_North_Carolina "New Hanover County, North Carolina") counties, and several other roads, with ten bridges destroyed.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-sog-40) More than 1,500 people required rescue from their flooded homes.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nws-37) Rail travel across the area was halted.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-sog-40) Flooding forced the [East Carolina Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Carolina_Pirates "East Carolina Pirates") to relocate their football game against [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Miami "University of Miami") to [N.C. State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NC_State_Wolfpack "NC State Wolfpack")'s [Carter–Finley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter%E2%80%93Finley_Stadium "Carter–Finley Stadium") in Raleigh.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-46) Some locations remained flooded for two months, after [Hurricane Irene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Irene_(1999) "Hurricane Irene (1999)") produced additional floods in October 1999.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ilm-43)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-usgs-41) Much of the western portion of the state remained under a severe drought.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-extremes0999-12)

When Floyd made landfall on North Carolina, the NHC estimated [maximum sustained winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_sustained_winds "Maximum sustained winds") of around 105 mph (169 km/h). The highest reported sustained wind was 64 mph (103 km/h) at [Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Corps_Air_Station_Cherry_Point "Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point"). Wind gusts were much higher, reaching 138 mph (222 km/h) in [Wrightsville Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrightsville_Beach,_North_Carolina "Wrightsville Beach, North Carolina"), at the elevation of an eight–story building. Other strong wind gusts included 122 mph (196 km/h) at [Topsail Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topsail_Beach,_North_Carolina "Topsail Beach, North Carolina"), and 120 mph (190 km/h) at the Wilmington Emergency Operations Center.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) The [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") issued 20[tornado warnings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_warning "Tornado warning") for the state.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-NCNCDC-17) Floyd spawned at least 16 tornadoes across eastern North Carolina. Ten of these occurred in the Wilmington area. In [Perquimans County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perquimans_County,_North_Carolina "Perquimans County, North Carolina"), a tornado destroyed two houses and damaged two others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) Along the Atlantic Coast, Albemarle Sound, and river basins, Floyd produced a significant [storm tide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_tide "Storm tide"). The highest water level in the state was 10.3 ft (3.1 m) on [Masonboro Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masonboro_Island "Masonboro Island").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) The hurricane caused significant [beach erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_erosion "Coastal erosion") along south-facing beaches. [Pine Knoll Shores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pine_Knoll_Shores "Pine Knoll Shores") lost about 50 ft (15 m) of sand. Two coastal piers lost significant sections from the waves. On [Ocracoke Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocracoke_Island "Ocracoke Island"), high tides washed away dunes at ten locations.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-NCNCDC-17) On [Oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Island_(North_Carolina) "Oak Island (North Carolina)") and [Topsail Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topsail_Island "Topsail Island"), the high waters damaged homes.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-usgs-41)

### Mid-Atlantic states

Flooding in Franklin, Virginia

The interaction of Floyd and a stalled [cold front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_front "Cold front") brought significant rainfall across the Mid-Atlantic states, as the storm produced strong wind gusts.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)

In Virginia, rainfall reached 16.57 in (421 mm) in [Newport News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_News "Newport News"), while the highest wind gust was 100 mph (160 km/h), recorded on the [James River Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_River_Bridge "James River Bridge").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-vancdc-47) The storm downed hundreds of power lines and trees, some centuries old.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-wpc-48) Statewide damage totaled $101 million, and there were four fatalities – two from fallen trees in [Fairfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax,_Virginia "Fairfax, Virginia") and [Halifax County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_County,_Virginia "Halifax County, Virginia"), one in a traffic accident in [Hanover County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanover_County "Hanover County"), and a man in [Accomack County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accomack_County "Accomack County") who drowned in his submerged vehicle.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-wpc-48) The heavy rains washed out several roads, and closed regional routes including [Interstate 95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_95_in_Virginia "Interstate 95 in Virginia") between [Emporia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emporia,_Virginia "Emporia, Virginia") and [Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersburg,_Virginia "Petersburg, Virginia"), [U.S. Route 58](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_58#Virginia "U.S. Route 58") between Emporia and [Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin,_Virginia "Franklin, Virginia"), and [U.S. Route 460](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_460_in_Virginia "U.S. Route 460 in Virginia") near [Wakefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakefield,_Virginia "Wakefield, Virginia").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-vancdc-47) The rainfall led to overflowing rivers in the [Chowan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chowan_River "Chowan River") Basin, some of which exceeded 500-year flood levels.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-usgs-flooding-45) The [Blackwater River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackwater_River_(Virginia) "Blackwater River (Virginia)") reached 100-year flood levels and flooded [Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin,_Virginia "Franklin, Virginia") with 12 ft (3.7 m) of water. Extensive road damage occurred there, isolating the area from the rest of the state. Some 182 businesses and 150 houses were underwater in Franklin from the worst flooding in 60 years. Two dams along the [Rappahannock River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rappahannock_River "Rappahannock River") burst from the extreme flooding. Throughout Virginia, Floyd damaged 9,250 houses.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-wpc-48) Along the Atlantic and Chesapeake Bay, Floyd produced a 5 to 7 ft (1.5 to 2.1 m) storm surge, causing coastal flooding.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-vancdc-47)

Wind gusts in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") reached 56 mph (90 km/h) at the [Children's National Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_National_Medical_Center "Children's National Medical Center"). The storm caused a shop on [New York Avenue NW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Avenue_(Washington,_D.C.) "New York Avenue (Washington, D.C.)") to close after the roof collapsed.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-wpc-48) The hurricane's rainbands moved across Maryland, dropping 12.59 in (320 mm) of rainfall in [Chestertown, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chestertown,_Maryland "Chestertown, Maryland").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Mid_Atl-49) About 450 people evacuated from low-lying areas. A mudslide in [Anne Arundel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Arundel_County,_Maryland "Anne Arundel County, Maryland") County stranded five trains carrying about 1,000 passengers. Flooding closed 225 roads statewide, with dozens of motorists requiring rescue, and more than 90 bridges were damaged. A man in [Centreville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centreville,_Maryland "Centreville, Maryland") died while attempting to jump a washed out bridge on his motorcycle. High tides, 2 to 3 ft (0.61 to 0.91 m) above normal, destroyed 5 houses and severely damaged 23 others. Flooding inundated the only bridge to [St. George Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George_Island,_Maryland "St. George Island, Maryland"), stranding six people. Wind gusts peaked at 71 mph (114 km/h) in [Tall Timbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tall_Timbers,_St._Mary's_County,_Maryland "Tall Timbers, St. Mary's County, Maryland").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-mdncdc-50)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ncdcmd2-20) The winds knocked down hundreds of trees, including the nearly 400 year–old Liberty Tree at [St. John's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._John's_College_(Annapolis/Santa_Fe) "St. John's College (Annapolis/Santa Fe)") in Annapolis.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-mdncdc-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-51) The winds also knocked down power lines, leaving about 500,000 customers without electricity. Two people were injured, and one person killed, from [Carbon monoxide poisoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide_poisoning "Carbon monoxide poisoning") related to using a generator. The Anne Arundel county fair was canceled for the first time in its history.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-mdncdc-50) Statewide damage was estimated at $7.9 million.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-52)

In Delaware, rainfall peaked at 12.58 in (320 mm) in [Greenwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwood,_Delaware "Greenwood, Delaware"), breaking the state's highest 24 hour rainfall total. The rains caused record crests along rivers and streams in [New Castle County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_County "New Castle County"). The [White Clay Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Clay_Creek "White Clay Creek") crested at 17.6 ft (5.4 m), and was above flood stage for 18 hours. Statewide damage totaled $8.42 million, including 171 damaged homes, and another 33 homes that were condemned. Flooding closed hundreds of roads and bridges, and dozens of motorists required rescue. The floods washed out two bridges and a few miles of track belonging to the [Wilmington and Western Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington_and_Western_Railroad "Wilmington and Western Railroad"). Winds in the state reached 64 mph (104 km/h) at [Cape Henlopen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Henlopen "Cape Henlopen"). The winds knocked down trees and power lines, leaving about 25,000 people without power.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Mid_Atl-49)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-dencdc-21)

Rainfall in New Jersey reached 14.13 in (359 mm) in [Little Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Falls,_New_Jersey "Little Falls, New Jersey").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Mid_Atl-49) Following the state's fourth-worst drought in a century,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-njem-53) the rains collected in rivers and streams, causing record flooding at 18 river gauges, and mostly affecting the [Raritan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raritan_River "Raritan River"), [Passaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passaic_River "Passaic River"), and [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") basins.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nyt1017-54)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-njncdc-22) Statewide damage totaled $250 million, much of it in [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_County,_New_Jersey "Somerset County, New Jersey") and [Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen_County,_New_Jersey "Bergen County, New Jersey") counties. This made Floyd the costliest [natural disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_disaster "Natural disaster") in New Jersey's history, until it was surpassed by [Hurricane Irene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Irene "Hurricane Irene") in 2011.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-55) Seven people died in New Jersey during Floyd's passage – six due to drowning, and one in a traffic accident. A police lieutenant took his life after working for nearly 48 hours coordinating floodwater rescues. In [Bound Brook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bound_Brook,_New_Jersey "Bound Brook, New Jersey"), the Raritan crested at a record 42.5 ft (13.0 m) on September 16, well above the 28 ft (8.5 m) flood stage, and exceeding the previous record of 37.5 ft (11.4 m) set during [Tropical Storm Doria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Doria "Tropical Storm Doria") in 1971. Downtown Bound Brook was flooded 13 ft (4.0 m), causing 200 buildings to be condemned. In [Manville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manville,_New_Jersey "Manville, New Jersey"), the Raritan crested at a record 27.5 ft (8.4 m), nearly double the flood stage of 14 ft (4.3 m). Parts of Manville were flooded to a depth of 10 ft (3.0 m), which damaged 1,500 homes, caused 284 homes to be condemned, and forced 1,000 people to evacuate. A [water treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_treatment "Water treatment") plant was damaged in [Bridgewater Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgewater_Township,_New_Jersey "Bridgewater Township, New Jersey"), forcing nearly 500,000 people in Hunterdon, [Mercer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_County,_New_Jersey "Mercer County, New Jersey"), [Middlesex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_County,_New_Jersey "Middlesex County, New Jersey"), and Somerset counties to boil water for eight days.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-njncdc-22)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nyt1017-54) The [Rochelle Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochelle_Park,_New_Jersey "Rochelle Park, New Jersey") hub of [Electronic Data Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Data_Systems "Electronic Data Systems") was inundated by the nearby [Saddle River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddle_River_(Passaic_River) "Saddle River (Passaic River)"), disrupting service to as many as 8,000 ATMs across the United States.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-rochelle_park_eds-56) Flooding in an adjoining [Bell Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Atlantic "Bell Atlantic") switching facility cut off phone service to 1 million customers in the area.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-rochelle_park_bell_atlantic-57)

In Pennsylvania, Floyd killed 13 people – four due to drownings, four from traffic accidents, three from heart-attacks, and two from fallen trees. Another 40 people were severely injured.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-pancdc-58) The storm dropped heavy rainfall across the state, peaking at 12.13 in (308 mm) in [Marcus Hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Hook,_Pennsylvania "Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Mid_Atl-49) The rains led to 100–year floods along rivers and streams in southeastern Pennsylvania. More than 10,000 homes were flooded, forcing about 7,000 people to evacuate. Hundreds of people required rescue from the floodwaters, using boats or jet-skis. About 400 people were stranded at the [Radisson Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radisson_Hotel "Radisson Hotel"). In [Conshohocken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conshohocken,_Pennsylvania "Conshohocken, Pennsylvania"), ten people evacuated an inundated train, but when the rescue boat capsized, they had to hold onto a tree. The floods damaged 1,000 homes and left another 200 homes destroyed or uninhabitable. More than 500 apartments and 100 businesses were also flooded. Floods from the [Darby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darby_Creek_(Pennsylvania) "Darby Creek (Pennsylvania)") and Cobb creeks, reaching 8 ft (2.4 m) deep, damaged parts of [Darby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darby,_Pennsylvania "Darby, Pennsylvania") in Delaware County. In [Aston Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Township,_Pennsylvania "Aston Township, Pennsylvania"), mud accumulated to 3 to 4 ft (0.91 to 1.22 m). Statewide damage was estimated around $60 million, of which one-third was related to infrastructure. Hundreds of roads and bridges were damaged or closed, including parts of the regional rail network. Runoff inundated treatments plants, causing raw sewage to empty into rivers. Tidal flooding also occurred in southeastern Pennsylvania. Wind gusts in the state reached 58 mph (93 km/h) at the [Commodore Barry Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodore_Barry_Bridge "Commodore Barry Bridge"). The combination of high winds and rains knocked down hundreds of trees and power lines, leaving about 501,000 customers without power. Downed trees also damaged the [Gibson's Covered Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibson's_Covered_Bridge "Gibson's Covered Bridge").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-pancdc-58) High winds knocked over several freight train cars along the [Rockville Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockville_Bridge "Rockville Bridge"), which spans the [Susquehanna River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susquehanna_River "Susquehanna River"); their contents did not spill.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-59)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Ts-floyd-19990916-2345utc.gif/250px-Ts-floyd-19990916-2345utc.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ts-floyd-19990916-2345utc.gif)

Tropical Storm Floyd over New England on September 16

In New York, rainfall peaked at 13.70 in (348 mm) in [Brewster, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster,_New_York "Brewster, New York").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) The rains produced floods that killed two people – a 9 year-old girl in [Wingdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wingdale,_New_York "Wingdale, New York"), and a 53 year-old man in [Orangetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orangetown,_New_York "Orangetown, New York").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nyncdc-23)[Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York") recorded their wettest day on record, with 5.6 in (140 mm) of rainfall.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-60) Rivers and tributaries flooded across New York, forcing 27 homes to evacuate and causing flood damage across four counties. Portions of a few roads, including a portion of [NY 32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Route_32 "New York State Route 32"), were washed out.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nyncdc-23) Wind gusts in the state peaked at 62 mph (100 km/h) in [Newburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburgh,_New_York "Newburgh, New York").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-tcr-2) The winds and heavy rains caused widespread tree and power line damage, leaving more than 100,000 people without electricity.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-nyncdc-23) A dam on a [mill pond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_pond "Mill pond") broke near [Lake Placid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Placid,_New_York "Lake Placid, New York"), leading to flooding along the Chubb River.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-impacts-61)

### New England

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: New England")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Floyd_1999_rainfall.gif/250px-Floyd_1999_rainfall.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Floyd_1999_rainfall.gif)

Rainfall in the United States and Canada

In Connecticut, the storm caused one casualty: a man drowned after boating in the swollen [Quinnipiac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinnipiac_River "Quinnipiac River").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-CTNC-62) Rainfall in the state peaked at 11.4 in (290 mm) in [West Hartford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Hartford,_Connecticut "West Hartford, Connecticut").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-New_Eng-63) Numerous rivers overflowed, including the [Still River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Still_River_(Housatonic_River) "Still River (Housatonic River)") and its tributaries, which triggered severe flooding. Floods in [Danbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danbury,_Connecticut "Danbury, Connecticut") were the worst in 40 years, where hundreds of homes and vehicles were damaged after floodwaters reached 4 ft (1.2 m) deep. Across the state, several roads and basements were inundated. Wind gusts exceeding 50 mph (80 km/h), combined with the saturated ground, brought down many trees and triggered severe power outages in the area. Damage totaled $2.4 million.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-CTNC-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Danbury-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-times-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-66) In neighboring Rhode Island, rainfall reached 7.12 in (181 mm) at [North Smithfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Smithfield,_Rhode_Island "North Smithfield, Rhode Island"), which caused the [Pawtuxet River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pawtuxet_River "Pawtuxet River") to slightly exceed flood stage. Storm tides were 5.6 ft (1.7 m) above normal in [Providence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island"), which inundated low-lying areas. The winds, peaking at 45 mph (72 km/h) in [Block Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_Island "Block Island"), knocked down trees and wires.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-67) In Massachusetts, wind gusts reached 76 mph (122 km/h) in [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"). The winds knocked downed trees and power lines, which closed roads near [Pittsfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsfield,_Massachusetts "Pittsfield, Massachusetts"). Rainfall in the state reached 9.16 in (233 mm) in [Southwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwick,_Massachusetts "Southwick, Massachusetts"). The rains flooded rivers and streams across western Massachusetts.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-New_Eng-63)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-69)

Rainfall across New England peaked at 11.53 in (293 mm) on [Mount Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Mansfield "Mount Mansfield") in Vermont.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-New_Eng-63) Wind gusts in the state peaked at 60 mph (97 km/h) in [Hardwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardwick,_Vermont "Hardwick, Vermont"). The combination of the winds and rainfall knocked down many trees, killing a camper in [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph,_Vermont "Randolph, Vermont"). In [Putney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putney,_Vermont "Putney, Vermont"), a driver was injured when a tree destroyed her vehicle. Thousands of people lost power, leading to school closures and the cancelation of the annual [Tunbridge World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunbridge_World's_Fair "Tunbridge World's Fair"). Downed trees also damaged hiking trails. The rains also produced floods that washed out a portion of [U.S. 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_5_in_Vermont "U.S. Route 5 in Vermont") in [Weathersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weathersfield,_Vermont "Weathersfield, Vermont").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-70) The storm produced 8 to 10 ft (2.4 to 3.0 m) waves along [Lake Champlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Champlain "Lake Champlain"), damaging a few boats and halting ferry service.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-71) In neighboring New Hampshire, rainfall peaked at 9.54 in (242 mm) on [Mount Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Washington "Mount Washington").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-New_Eng-63) Wind gusts in the state reached 47 mph (76 km/h) in [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth,_New_Hampshire "Portsmouth, New Hampshire"). The combination of winds and rains downed trees and power lines, leaving 10,000 people in the state without power. There was also minor flooding.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-72) In Maine, the precipitation peaked at 8.72 in (221 mm) in [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland,_Maine "Poland, Maine").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-New_Eng-63) The rains inundated a few basements and roads. Wind gusts reached 40 mph (65 km/h) in Maine, causing scattered power outages.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-73)

### Canada

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Canada")]

The remnants of Floyd produced rainfall and gusty winds from Ontario to [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada"), with 118 km/h (73 mph) occurring along the [Saint Lawrence River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Lawrence_River "Saint Lawrence River") in Quebec, the strongest winds in the country.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ec-26) The high winds damaged corn and other crops along the river's south shore from the [l'Amiante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Amiante "L'Amiante") to [Bellechasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellechasse_Regional_County_Municipality,_Quebec "Bellechasse Regional County Municipality, Quebec") regions.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-QC-74) The highest rainfall in Canada also occurred in eastern Quebec, reaching 4.8 in (122 mm). Power outages affected Montreal and Quebec City, causing classes to be canceled at the [Université de Montréal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_de_Montr%C3%A9al "Université de Montréal"). Inclement weather was a potential factor in a five car accident on [Autoroute 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_Autoroute_15 "Quebec Autoroute 15") in Montreal. Minor traffic accidents also occurred in the Maritimes. Heavy rainfall backed up storm drains in [Fredericton, New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredericton,_New_Brunswick "Fredericton, New Brunswick"). The [Confederation Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederation_Bridge "Confederation Bridge") connecting [Prince Edward Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Edward_Island "Prince Edward Island") to the mainland shut down during the storm due to 72 miles per hour (116 km/h) winds. About 6,000 people lost power in Nova Scotia.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-ec-26)

## Aftermath

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

### The Bahamas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: The Bahamas")]

To help the affected citizens, the [Bahamas Red Cross Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas_Red_Cross_Society?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bahamas Red Cross Society (page does not exist)") opened 41 shelters, though within one week many returned home.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-75) The Bahamas required $435,000 (1999 USD; $840,716 2026 USD) in aid following the storm, much of it in food parcels.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-baha-29) The [Inter-American Development Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-American_Development_Bank "Inter-American Development Bank") loaned $21 million (1999 USD; $40.6 million 2026 USD) to the archipelago to restore bridges, roads, seawalls, docks, and other building projects in the aftermath of the hurricane.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-76)

### United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: United States")]

Then-President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") designated several counties as federal disaster areas, including 11 in Florida, 6 in Georgia, 66 in North Carolina, 43[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-77) in Virginia, 11 in Maryland, 1 in Delaware, 8 in Pennsylvania, 9 in New Jersey, 4 in New York, 3 in Connecticut, 10 in Vermont, 3 in New Hampshire, and 5 in Maine.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-sog-40)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-78)

### North Carolina

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: North Carolina")]

[![Image 18: A satellite image depicting run-off offshore of North Carolina](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Floyd_runoff.png/250px-Floyd_runoff.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Floyd_runoff.png)

Runoff in the aftermath of the hurricane

Across eastern North Carolina, residents were advised to boil water due to water contamination; this included seven communities that still had to boil water by the end of November 1999.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-sog-40) In describing Floyd's effects, North Carolina's Secretary of Health and Human Services, H. David Bruton, stated, "nothing since the Civil War has been as destructive to families here."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-extremes0999-12) In the 44 counties that sustained the most damage, about 75% of businesses temporarily closed, averaging 5–8 days. The lost revenue was estimated around $4 billion. About 31,000 people lost their jobs, and around 17% of small businesses lacked flood insurance.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-79)

Runoff from the hurricane created significant problems for the ecology of North Carolina's rivers and sounds. In the immediate aftermath of the storm, freshwater runoff, sediment, and decomposing organic matter caused salinity and oxygen levels in [Pamlico Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamlico_Sound "Pamlico Sound") and its tributary rivers to drop to nearly zero. This raised fears of massive fish and shrimp kills, as had happened after [Hurricane Fran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fran "Hurricane Fran") and [Hurricane Bonnie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Bonnie_(1998) "Hurricane Bonnie (1998)"), and the state government responded quickly to provide financial aid to fishing and shrimping industries. Strangely, however, the year's shrimp and crab harvests were extremely prosperous; one possible explanation is that runoff from [Hurricane Dennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dennis_(1999) "Hurricane Dennis (1999)") caused marine animals to begin migrating to saltier waters, so they were less vulnerable to Floyd's ill effects.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-Legacy-1) Pollution from runoff was also a significant fear. Numerous pesticides were found in low but measurable quantities in the river waters, particularly in the Neuse River. Overall, however, the concentration of contaminants was slightly lower than had been measured in Hurricane Fran, likely because Floyd simply dropped more water to dilute them.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-usgs-flooding-45)

When the hurricane hit North Carolina, it flooded hog waste lagoons and released 25 million gallons of manure into the rivers, which contaminated the water supply and reduced water quality.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-80)[Ronnie Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Kennedy?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ronnie Kennedy (page does not exist)"), Duplin County director for environmental health, said that of 310 private wells he had tested for contamination since the storm, 9 percent, or three times the average across eastern North Carolina, had fecal coliform bacteria. Normally, tests showing any hint of feces in drinking water, an indication that it can be carrying disease-causing pathogens, are cause for immediate action.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-81)

FEMA opened 16 disaster recovery centers and a mobile office to assist residents with the application process. The federal government deployed 797 employees to North Carolina, including more than 400 housing inspectors.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-FEMA_Glance-82) By a year after Floyd struck North Carolina, the state and federal government had provided $1.9 billion worth of assistance. The largest assistance program was $503 million in low-interest loans from the Small Business Administration, for 12,863 renters, homeowners, and business owners. State and federal resources provided $306.5 million in direct housing assistance. The [National Flood Insurance Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Flood_Insurance_Program "National Flood Insurance Program") paid more than $143 million to 12,843 residents who lost their properties due to floods. For uninsured residents who did not qualify for loans, FEMA provided $92.1 million to 23,873 households in grants. FEMA also provided 2,535[trailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(towed_trailer) "Caravan (towed trailer)") for displaced residents, at the cost of $48 million. The federal government authorized $133.1 million to cover 75% of the cost of repairing and rebuilding public facilities. The Hazard Mitigation Grant Program spent $149.1 million to purchase 2,074 flooded homes and tear them down, preserving the land instead as green space. At the time, it was the largest building buyout program in American history.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-fem1-83)[Rocky Mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mount,_North_Carolina "Rocky Mount, North Carolina") had the largest buyout in the state, with 446 homes bought and torn down.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-84)

The Hurricane Floyd disaster was followed by what many judged to be a very slow federal response. Fully three weeks after the storm hit, [Jesse Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Jackson "Jesse Jackson") complained to [FEMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FEMA "FEMA") Director [James Lee Witt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lee_Witt "James Lee Witt") on his [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") program _Both Sides Now_, "It seemed there was preparation for Hurricane Floyd, but then came Flood Floyd. Bridges are overwhelmed, levees are overwhelmed, whole towns under water ... [it's] an awesome scene of tragedy. So there's a great misery index in North Carolina." Witt responded, "We're starting to move the camper trailers in. It's been so wet it's been difficult to get things in there, but now it's going to be moving very quickly. And I think you're going to see a—I think the people there will see a big difference [within] this next weekend."[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Pennsylvania

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Pennsylvania")]

In Pennsylvania, 16,442 FEMA applications were received, and by November 19, $26.6 million in aid had been provided.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-85)[Catholic Charities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Charities "Catholic Charities") provided additional assistance to North Carolina, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-86)

### Retirement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hurricane_Floyd&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Retirement")]

See also: [list of retired Atlantic hurricane names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_retired_Atlantic_hurricane_names "List of retired Atlantic hurricane names")

Due to the high impact, extensive damage, and loss of life from the hurricane, the [name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_naming "Tropical cyclone naming")_Floyd_ was retired by the [World Meteorological Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Meteorological_Organization "World Meteorological Organization") in the spring of 2000, and it will never again be used for another north Atlantic tropical cyclone. It was replaced with _Franklin_ for the [2005 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2005 Atlantic hurricane season").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Floyd#cite_note-87)
